transcript: The two things I hear the most often are the economy and the condition of the Sierra Nevada. My district pretty much is the Sierra Nevada of California. From that, we produced a steady stream of revenue and commerce for the region that supported our local communities, supported thriving economies throughout the Sierra. When we passed laws in the 1970s that made the management of our forests all but impossible, we've watched them do what an untended garden will do, and that is grow and grow until it chokes itself to death. And of course the economy, now we have that tremendous success there. The tax reductions and regulatory reforms that we've been able to win over the last couple of years are produced one of the most profound economic expansions in our nation's history. and we're seeing that across the country. Lowest unemployment rate in 50 years. Lowest unemployment rate for women since the 1950s. Lowest unemployment rate for Americans of African and Hispanic descent since they began keeping records. So we've had some significant successes there. We've had some successes in forest management. We need to get those same reforms enacted for the entire national forest system, but I think we can now make a pretty good case on that.

transcript: Well, exactly. And I was struck by something that Jerry Brown said after the campfire that wiped out the town of Paradise, killed 86 people. He said, well, this is the new abnormal. And I went back and did some looking at that and found out it's not the new abnormal at all. It's the old normal. In the last half of the 20th century, We lost about 250,000 acres a year in California to catastrophic fire. It was very steady, very consistent, about 250,000 acres. Last year, we lost one and a half million acres to catastrophic wildfire. something very bad has happened. But when we look at the destruction of paradise, we forget that was about 150,000 acres. In 1910, the big burn destroyed three million acres in Montana and Idaho, wiped out six towns and killed 87 people among a much sparser population than we have today. It was right around that time that we formed the US Forest Service. The Forest Service's job was to protect the forest, to manage them properly. And as I said, an untended forest is like an untended garden. If you leave it alone and don't tend to it, it's going to choke itself to death and ultimately will be consumed by catastrophic fire. And if you go back into the pre-Columbian days, you'll see that's exactly what happened. Prior to the discovery of California, the paleontologists tell us that in California, we would lose between 4.5 million and 12 million acres a year to catastrophic fire. That's what happens when the forests aren't properly managed. That's nature's way of dealing with it. Because of good management, we brought that from between four and a half and 12 million acres a year down to only a quarter million. When we abandoned those policies in the 1970s, we've watched the acreage being consumed by fire grow dramatically. We've seen an 80% decline in timber harvested off the federal lands over the past 30 years since those laws took effect 40 years now. And we've also watched a concomitant increase in acres destroyed by fire. There's an old maxim that excess timber comes out of a forest one way or another. It's either carried out or it burns out, but it will come out. When we carried it out, we had healthy forests. We also had a thriving local economy. And since we consigned our forests back to a policy of benign neglect, we've watched them consumed by fire.

transcript: Well, first let's just get a brief background of our water situation. Fortunately, we live in one of the most water-rich regions of the country in northern California. But, you know, everybody seems to think that the Colorado River is the great river in the West. Colorado River is a junior sister of the Sacramento. The Sacramento is a much, much larger river. The difference is we store 70 million acre feet of water on the Colorado. We only store 10 million acre feet on the Sacramento and lose most of the rest of that to the Pacific Ocean every year. What I learned, chairing the water committee for four years, is that droughts are nature's fault. They happen. But water shortages are our fault. Water shortages are a result of deliberate choice that we made to stop building dams. And the reason we stop building dams is because of the same environmental laws that have made the management of our forests impossible has also made the construction of new reservoirs cost prohibitive. We have not added a major reservoir over a million acre feet to our water system in California in the last, well, since 1979. Meanwhile, the population has nearly doubled. We're not going to solve our water shortages until we build more dams, and we're not going to build more dams until we overhaul the laws that have made their construction impossible. I'm just to give you one example. I've got the town of Forest Hill in my district. They get their water from a small reservoir called the Sugar Pine Reservoir, built years ago with an 18-foot spillway, but no spillway gate. didn't need the extra water at the time due now.
